### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by the Legislature

Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing percentage of votes needed to approve such ballot measures from a majority (over 50%) to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. **Fiscal Impact:** Possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future due to a higher vote threshold for certain taxes. **Supporters:** California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce **Opponents:** California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

YES A YES vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.

 

### ARGUMENTS

PRO Prop. 43 protects taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes, including sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters. Vote yes.

CON PROPOSITION 43 LIMITS VOTERS’ ABILITY TO FUND ESSENTIAL LOCAL SERVICES including fire protection, 911 response, schools, roads, hospitals and affordable housing. Currently, local governments must obtain two-thirds voter approval to impose, extend, or increase special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose) that they place on the ballot. Put on the ballot by the Legislature. Limits voters’ ability to pass voter-proposed local special taxes by increasing the percentage of votes needed from a majority to two-thirds, beginning January 1, 2027. Fiscal impact as noted above.

**Supporters:** California Taxpayers Association; Family Business Association of California; California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.  
**Opponents:** California Professional Firefighters; California Federation of Teachers; Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.[[2]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/43.htm)

**What your vote means:**  
- **YES:** Certain local government taxes would require two-thirds approval by voters.  
- **NO:** Certain local government taxes could continue to be approved by voters with a majority vote.[[2]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/43.htm)

### Analysis by the Legislative Analyst
**Background:** California has many local governments (cities, counties, special districts, and school districts). The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board. Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote, while others require a majority. Some increases are permanent; others are for a limited time and can be extended by voters.

**Proposal:** Under current law, local taxes used for a specific purpose (special taxes) require a two-thirds vote. Recent court decisions have allowed special taxes *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

**Fiscal effects:** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. ### Arguments and Rebuttals

This has led to over 2,000 new or higher local taxes in the past decade, increasing costs for families, homeowners, renters, and small businesses. It guarantees the right to vote on all local taxes, requires two-thirds approval for special taxes, and ensures funds are spent as promised. ## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***Local Governments in California.*** California has many local governments. These include cities, counties, special districts, and school districts.

***Vote Thresholds for Local Taxes.*** The State Constitution allows local governments to increase taxes with local voter approval. Tax increases can be put on a ballot by voters or a local governing board (such as a city council or board of supervisors). Increases in some types of local taxes require a two-thirds vote to approve them, while other types of taxes require a majority (more than half) vote to approve them. Some local tax increases are approved permanently, while others are approved for a limited period of time. Before those taxes expire, voters can be asked whether to extend them.

### PROPOSAL

***Requires Certain Local Taxes Receive Two-Thirds Approval by Voters.*** Under current law, local taxes that are used for a specific purpose require a two-thirds vote to be approved. These are called special taxes. However, recent court decisions have allowed special taxes that are *proposed by voters* to be approved with a majority vote. Under Proposition 43, beginning on January 1, 2027, any new, increased, or extended local special taxes proposed by voters would require a two-thirds vote.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***Possibility for Lower Local Government Tax Revenues in the Future.*** Proposition 43 makes it harder for local governments to pass certain taxes. As a result, local governments’ tax revenues could be lower in the future than they otherwise would be. The actual revenue impact is unknown and would depend on future decisions by local governments and voters.

Proposition 43 (2026)

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Flag_of_California.svg/60px-Flag_of_California.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)* * *

**November 3, 2026**

**Restoration Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Initiative Special Taxes Amendment**

**Proposition 43** is a proposed [legislative constitutional amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_amendment "Constitutional amendment") on the November 3, 2026, ballot in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California").

Starting on January 1, 2027, Proposition 43 would restore the two-thirds voter approval requirement to impose, extend, or increase a local special (legally dedicated) tax under [Proposition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_California_Proposition_13 "1978 California Proposition 13") for any proposed special tax that qualifies for the ballot under the local [initiative power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_initiative "Popular initiative").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) Proposition 43 would also prohibit local governments, including under the local initiative power, from imposing additional ad valorem taxes on real property (taxes based on the assessed value of property), except as otherwise allowed under the [California Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_California "Constitution of California").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)

Proposition 43 was proposed to overturn appellate court rulings following the 2017 *Upland* decision by the [California Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_California "Supreme Court of California"),[\[3\]](#cite_note-Upland-3) which created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the two-thirds voter approval requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13. These appellate court rulings held that citizen-led special tax proposals under the local initiative power were no longer subject to the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13.

Proposition 43 was placed on the ballot by [legislative referral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legislative_referral "Legislative referral")[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) with bipartisan support from both Democrats and Republicans in the [California State Legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") by a 68–2 vote in the [California State Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Assembly "California State Assembly") and by a 35–1 vote in the [California State Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Senate "California State Senate").[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

On three previous occasions, California voters approved the two-thirds voter approval requirement for all local special taxes when they adopted the Proposition 13 initiative constitutional amendment in 1978, the Proposition 62 statutory initiative in 1986, and the [Proposition 218](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_California_Proposition_218 "1996 California Proposition 218") (“Right to Vote on Taxes Act”) initiative constitutional amendment in 1996.

In 1987, a California appellate court in the *Altadena Library* case held that the two-thirds voter approval requirement for local special taxes under Proposition 13 *applied* to a local initiative special tax increase proposed by the electorate under the local initiative power.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The *Altadena Library* case was later cited with approval by the California Supreme Court in a 1995 case upholding the statutory voter approval requirements for local taxes under Proposition 62 (a 1986 taxpayer protection initiative measure), including the two-thirds voter approval requirement for local special taxes.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) Following the *Altadena Library* case, California law was clear for decades that local special tax initiatives were subject to two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13.

### 2017 *Upland* decision and later court rulings

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 2017 Upland decision and later court rulings")\]

In the 2017 [*Upland* case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_California_Proposition_218#Application_of_Proposition_218_to_local_tax_initiatives_\(2017_Upland_decision\) "1996 California Proposition 218") relating to Proposition 218 (“Right to Vote on Taxes Act”—a constitutional follow-up to Proposition 13), a divided California Supreme Court created a distinction between taxes proposed by the governing body of a local government and taxes proposed under the local initiative power for purposes of applying the voter approval requirements under constitutional taxpayer protection laws such as Proposition 13.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Upland-3)

The *Upland* decision was controversial and had an extensive dissenting opinion written by Justice [Leondra Kruger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leondra_Kruger "Leondra Kruger") and joined by Justice [Goodwin Liu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwin_Liu "Goodwin Liu"), both of whom were appointed by former Democratic Governor [Jerry Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brown "Jerry Brown").[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) In her dissenting opinion, Justice Kruger wrote that the voters never intended to distinguish between taxes placed on the ballot by the governing body and those proposed under the initiative power so as to create an exemption from Proposition 13 voter approval requirements for special tax increases proposed under the local initiative power.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

Local special taxes placed on the ballot by a local governing body such as a city council or a county board of supervisors are subject to two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) However, the majority opinion in th*e Upland* case contained ambiguous language on whether or not the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 applied to citizen-led special tax initiatives. This ambiguity led to lower appellate courts subsequently ruling that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes under Proposition 13 does *not* apply to citizen-led initiatives.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) To date, the California Supreme Court has refused to clarify the ambiguous language contained in its 2017 *Upland* decision or to resolve the conflict with the 1987 *Altadena Library* case which applied the two-thirds voter approval requirement under Proposition 13 to a local initiative special tax.

For special tax measures proposed under the local initiative power, the *Upland* decision took away from voters their constitutional right to vote on local special taxes under Proposition 13, a constitutional right that was previously recognized in the 1987 *Altadena Library* case.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The primary purpose of Proposition 43 is to restore that constitutional right to vote under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power.

As a result of the appellate court rulings following the *Upland* decision, many local initiative special tax increases passed *without* two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13. These include the Measure ULA (2022) “mansion tax” in [Los Angeles,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles")[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) the Proposition C business tax in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco,_CA "San Francisco, CA"), and numerous local sales and property tax increases. 

### Proposed initiative constitutional amendment

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Proposed initiative constitutional amendment")\]

In response to local special tax increases imposed without two-thirds voter approval under Proposition 13, an initiative constitutional amendment known as the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” was filed and later obtained sufficient signatures to appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot in California.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)

The “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative contained several integrated components that included: (1) restoring the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power; (2) significantly limiting the ability of local governments to impose real property transfer taxes like the Measure ULA "mansion tax" in Los Angeles; (3) ending existing initiative parcel taxes enacted without two-thirds voter approval; and (4) ending existing real property transfer taxes levied in [charter cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_rule_in_the_United_States#Home_rule_charter_cities "Home rule in the United States"), including the Measure ULA “mansion tax” in Los Angeles.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)

### Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=2026_California_Proposition_43&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise")\]

Ultimately, a bipartisan compromise was reached that resulted in the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative being withdrawn from the ballot by the initiative proponent[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) in favor of a more limited proposed constitutional amendment (ACA 22) that was placed on the ballot by the California Legislature and became known as Proposition 43.

Under the Proposition 43 bipartisan compromise, only the measure that would restore the two-thirds vote requirement under Proposition 13 for special taxes proposed under the local initiative power will appear on the November 2026 ballot for California voters to decide. Other components of the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative would not appear on the November 2026 ballot, including the limitations on real property transfer taxes and the provisions ending any already existing local taxes, including the Measure ULA “mansion tax” in Los Angeles.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) In exchange for withdrawing the “Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13” initiative, the Legislature also agreed to remove another proposed legislative constitutional amendment from the ballot (ACA 13) that would have made taxpayer protection constitutional amendments containing supermajority vote requirements much harder for California voters to approve.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)

## Key Findings

Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.

These are the key findings of the *Californians and their Government* survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:

*   **Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race.** Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
*   **Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label.** Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
*   **![Figure - Top state issues chosen by Californians](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/survey-1026_key-findings_fig1.png)Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today.** Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
*   **![Figure - Top national issues chosen by Californians](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='385'%20height='149'%20viewBox='0%200%20385%20149'%3E%3C/svg%3E)Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today.** Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.

## November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures

Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.

**Gubernatorial Election.** California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our [July survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.

![Figure - Xavier Becerra leads Steve Hilton by a wide margin in the governor's race](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='652'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20652'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% [October 2022 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/)), and the 2018 general election (60% [October 2018 survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).

About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our [May survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in [October 2022](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in [October 2018](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.

**House Races.** When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in [September](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), [July](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).

![Figure - A solid majority of California likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate if the 2026 election for the House of Representatives were held today](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='644'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20644'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in [May,](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in [September 2024](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

**Legislative Ballot Measures.** We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.

*   **Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs).** Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
*   **Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund).** Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
*   **Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns).** Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
*   **Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers).** Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
*   **Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services).** Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 43 varies across partisan groups (28% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 41% independents) and age groups (30% 18 to 34; 37% 35 to 54; 50% 55 and older) and is below 50 percent across regions.

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the [September survey](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).

![Table - Majorities of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 1 (Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (Rainy Day Fund)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='1622'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%201622'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

## Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot

In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).

After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).

![Figure - A majority of California likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes)](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='596'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20596'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.

A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.

Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.

Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.

## State of the State

Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.

When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.

Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since [June 2023](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.

![Figure - A majority of Californians think things in the state are generally going in the wrong direction](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='978'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20978'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.

With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in [February](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).

![Figure - Three in four feel their income is not keeping up with inflation](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='852'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20852'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since [October 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.

Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last [October](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in [May](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.

When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.

## State of the Nation

Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.

A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October [ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.

![Figure - Eight in ten Californians think things in the nation are generally going in the wrong direction](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='978'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20978'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.

Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.

When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.

![Figure - Most Californians are not satisfied with how democracy is working in the United States](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20width='1200'%20height='638'%20viewBox='0%200%201200%20638'%3E%3C/svg%3E)

About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in [October 2018](https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.

Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since [June 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.

Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.

Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October [Reuters/Ipsos](https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.

Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since [October 2025](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.

About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from [October 2024](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

## Methodology

The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.

Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The DSF-based sampling frame used for address selection is enhanced with a series of refinements—such as the appendage of various ancillary data to each address from commercial and government data sources—to facilitate complex stratification plans. Taking advantage of such refinements, quarterly samples are selected using a stratified sampling methodology that aims to retain the representativeness of the panel. KnowledgePanel recruits new panel members throughout the year to offset panel attrition.

To qualify for the survey, a panel member must be age 18 or older and reside in California. A general population sample of Californians was selected using Ipsos’s PPS (probability proportional to size) sampling procedure to select study-specific samples. Briefly, to select such samples, the panel is first weighted to population benchmarks and those panel weights are used as the measure of size for a PPS sample selection that yields a fully representative sample. A total of 1,800 respondents completed the survey out of 3,046 panelists who were sampled, for a response rate of 59 percent. To ensure the highest data quality, we flagged respondents who sped through the survey, which we defined as completing the survey in one-fourth of the overall median time (less than 3.5 minutes). We also flagged respondents if their self-reported age or gender did not match the data stored in their profile. A total of 72 cases were removed after this review process, resulting in 1,728 total qualified and valid cases.

Accent on Languages, Inc., translated new survey questions into Spanish, with assistance from Renatta DeFever.

We use the US Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey’s (ACS) Public Use Microdata Series for California (with regional coding information from the University of Minnesota’s Integrated Public Use Microdata Series for California) to compare certain demographic characteristics of the survey sample—region, age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and income—with the characteristics of California’s adult population. The survey sample was closely comparable to the ACS figures. We also used voter registration data from the California Secretary of State to compare the party registration of registered voters in our sample to party registration statewide. The sample of Californians is first weighted using an initial sampling or base weight that corrects for any differences in the probability of selecting various segments of the KnowledgePanel sample. This base weight is further adjusted using an iterative proportional fitting (raking) procedure that aligns sample demographics to population benchmarks from the 2024 ACS data as well as party registration benchmarks from the California Secretary of State’s voter registration file.

The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample of 1,728 adults. This means that 95 times out of 100, the results will be within 3 percentage points of what they would be if all adults in California were interviewed. The sampling error for unweighted subgroups is larger: for the 1,449 registered voters, the sampling error is ±3.3 percent; for the 1,086 likely voters, it is ±3.8 percent. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording, question order, and survey timing.

We present results for five geographic regions, accounting for approximately 90 percent of the state population. “Central Valley” includes Butte, Colusa, El Dorado, Fresno, Glenn, Kern, Kings, Madera, Merced, Placer, Sacramento, San Joaquin, Shasta, Stanislaus, Sutter, Tehama, Tulare, Yolo, and Yuba Counties. “San Francisco Bay Area” includes Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma Counties. “Los Angeles” refers to Los Angeles County, “Inland Empire” refers to Riverside and San Bernardino Counties, and “Orange/San Diego” refers to Orange and San Diego Counties. Residents of other geographic areas are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes for these less-populous areas are not large enough to report separately.

We present results for non-Hispanic whites, who account for 35 percent of the state’s adult population, and also for Latinos, who account for 38 percent of the state’s adult population and constitute one of the fastest-growing voter groups. We also present results for non-Hispanic Asian Americans, who make up about 17 percent of the state’s adult population, and non-Hispanic African Americans, who comprise about 5 percent. Results for other racial/ethnic groups—such as Native Americans—are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes are not large enough for separate analysis. Results for African American and Asian American likely voters are combined with those of other racial/ethnic groups because sample sizes for African American and Asian American likely voters are too small for separate analysis. We compare the opinions of those who report they are registered Democrats, registered Republicans, and decline-to-state or independent voters; the results for those who say they are registered to vote in other parties are not large enough for separate analysis. We also analyze the responses of likely voters—so designated per their responses to survey questions about voter registration, previous election participation, intentions to vote this year, attention to election news, and current interest in politics.

## Questions and Responses

October 16–22, 2026

 **California Proposition 43**, the **Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives and Property Tax Initiative Prohibition Amendment**, is on the [ballot](/California_2026_ballot_measures "California 2026 ballot measures") in [California](/California "California") as a [legislatively referred constitutional amendment](/Legislatively_referred_constitutional_amendment "Legislatively referred constitutional amendment") on [November 3, 2026](/California_2026_ballot_measures "California 2026 ballot measures").[\[1\]](#cite_note-Overview-1)[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

A "**yes**" vote supports this amendment to:

*   require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to be enacted and
*   prohibit local jurisdictions and ballot initiatives from enacting ad valorem property taxes, except for voter-approved bond debt-service taxes authorized elsewhere in the state constitution.

A "**no**" vote opposes this amendment to require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a two-thirds (66.67%) vote to be enacted, thereby maintaining that only a simple majority vote (50%+1) is required to enact initiated local special taxes.

## Overview

### How would Proposition 43 change the vote requirements for local special tax initiatives?

*See also: [Text of measure](#Text_of_measure)*

The initiative would amend the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution") to require that local ballot measures proposing, extending, or increasing special taxes initiated by citizens receive a [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") to be enacted. Currently, local special tax measures can be enacted in two ways: 1) a local governing board sends the tax to voters, and it is approved by a two-thirds vote, or 2) citizens can petition to place a special tax on local ballots, and it is approved by a simple majority of voters.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

The amendment would also prohibit any local government from levying ad valorem taxes on real property, including by ballot initiative, except for those authorized under [Article XIII](/Article_XIII,_California_Constitution "Article XIII, California Constitution") and [Article XIII A](/Article_XIII_A,_California_Constitution "Article XIII A, California Constitution"), which establishes a 1% base tax on real property and authorizes additional voter-approved bond debt-service property taxes.[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

### How did Proposition 43 get on the ballot?

*See also: [Path to the ballot](#Path_to_the_ballot)*

Proposition 43 was placed on the ballot as part of a legislative compromise between Democratic state leaders and petitioners sponsoring [another initiative](/California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)") that would have increased the vote requirement to pass citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority to a two-thirds vote; prohibited charter cities from imposing their own real estate transfer taxes, whether for general or specific purposes, above the existing statutory rate of $0.275 per $500 of value; and invalidated any property-related special taxes previously adopted with an approval rate below two-thirds or real estate transfer taxes in charter cities. California state law allows initiative sponsors to withdraw qualified initiatives until the ballot finalization deadline, which is 131 days before the election. The initiative was withdrawn from the ballot after the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") passed [Proposition 43](#Path_to_the_ballot) on June 25 — the 2026 ballot finalization deadline. It passed the state Assembly by a vote of 68-2, with nine not voting. It passed the state Senate by a vote of 35-1, with four not voting.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Overview-1) 

### What are supporters and opponents saying about Proposition 43?

*See also: [Support](#Support) and [Opposition](#Opposition)*

Jon Coupal, president of Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, which sponsored the [withdrawn initiative](#California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\)), said, "In 2024, the California Legislature sought to make it easier to raise taxes with Proposition 5, which the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association defeated at the ballot. Today the Legislature voted to make it harder to raise taxes by advancing a constitutional amendment, ACA 22, to close a loophole that had allowed some special taxes to pass with less than the two-thirds vote required by Proposition 13."[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) 

State Asm. [Buffy Wicks](/Buffy_Wicks "Buffy Wicks") (D-14), who authored Proposition 43, came out in opposition to the amendment. She said, "I authored ACA 22 not because I wanted it to become law — but because it was the only path left to get the more dangerous initiative off the ballot before time ran out." Evolve California, which also opposes Proposition 43, said, "If this measure passes, it will make California the hardest place in the country to raise local revenue."[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)

### Constitutional changes

*See also: [Article XIII A, California Constitution](/Article_XIII_A,_California_Constitution "Article XIII A, California Constitution")*

The ballot measure would add [Section 4.5 to Article XIII A](/Article_XIII_A,_California_Constitution "Article XIII A, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution"). The following underlined text would be added:[\[2\]](#cite_note-Text-2) 

*Note*: Hover over the text and scroll to see the full text. 

SEC. 4.5. (a) Beginning on January 1, 2027, and notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose, extend, or increase any special tax, except as provided in Section 4 of this article, subdivision (d) of Section 2 of Article XIII C, and paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D, unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.

  

(b) Notwithstanding Article II and Article XI, no local government, including the electorate of a local government exercising the initiative power, may impose ad valorem taxes on real property, except as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3 of Article XIII D.

  

(c) “Local government” and “special tax” shall have the same meaning as provided in Section 1 of Article XIII C.

## Prediction markets

*See also: [Prediction markets](/Prediction_markets "Prediction markets")*

A prediction market is a platform where users buy and sell contracts tied to the outcome of future events. The price of a contract reflects the market's estimated probability of that outcome — a contract priced at 55 cents suggests the market estimates a 55 percent chance the event occurs. Volume reflects how actively a market is being traded.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) Unlike polls, which survey a sample of voters, prediction markets aggregate the financial stakes of individual bettors. A market with higher trading volume is generally considered more reliable than one with low volume, though prices can be influenced by large individual traders. 

This section displays the contract prices on the outcome of this election from Kalshi, one of several prediction market platforms. Ballotpedia displays prediction market data for informational purposes; these markets do not predict election outcomes with certainty.

## Background

### General tax vs. special tax

[Section 1 of Article XIII C](/Article_XIII_C,_California_Constitution#Section_1 "Article XIII C, California Constitution") of the [California Constitution](/California_Constitution "California Constitution") defines a *general tax* as "any tax imposed for general governmental purposes." The section defines *special tax* as "any tax imposed for specific purposes, including a tax imposed for specific purposes, which is placed into a general fund." A *tax* is defined as "any levy, charge, or exaction of any kind imposed by a local government."[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) 

### California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)

*See also: [California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)](/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_\(June_1978\) "California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)")*

In 1978, California voters approved [Proposition 13](/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_\(June_1978\) "California Proposition 13, Tax Limitations Initiative (June 1978)") by a margin of 65% to 35%. The initiated constitutional amendment required local governments to refer special taxes to the ballot and required a two-thirds vote of electors. The amendment also:[\[13\]](#cite_note-taxdata-13) 

*   required that properties be taxed at no more than 1% of their full cash value shown on the 1975-1976 assessment rolls;
*   limited annual increases of assessed (taxable) value to the inflation rate or 2%, whichever was less;
*   allowed properties to be reassessed at 1% of their sale price upon property transfer and reset the limit on annual increases of assessed value;
*   prohibited the state legislature from enacting new taxes on the value or sale of properties;
*   require a two-thirds vote of the state legislature to increase non-property taxes; and
*   make the state government responsible for distributing property tax revenue among local governments.

[Howard Jarvis](/Howard_Jarvis "Howard Jarvis"), the founder of the [Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association](/Howard_Jarvis_Taxpayers_Association "Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association"), and Paul Gann, who developed the [Gann Limit](/California_Proposition_98,_Mandatory_Education_Spending_Initiative_\(1988\) "California Proposition 98, Mandatory Education Spending Initiative (1988)"), were proponents of the initiative.[\[14\]](#cite_note-14)[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) 

### California Proposition 218, Voter Approval Requirement for Local Tax Increases Initiative (1996)

*See also: [California Proposition 218 (1996)](#California_Proposition_218,_Voter_Approval_Requirement_for_Local_Tax_Increases_Initiative_\(1996\))*

In 1996, California voters approved Proposition 218 by a vote of 56.5% to 43.5%. Proposition 218 required local governments to refer ordinances to impose taxes or property-related assessments, fees, and charges to the ballot for voter consideration. It also required that elections for general taxes be held at regular elections and required a two-thirds supermajority vote of approval for special taxes. 

#### Lawsuits regarding Proposition 218 vote requirements

An August 2017 [California Supreme Court decision](/Laws_governing_local_ballot_measures_in_California#Taxes_imposed_by_citizen_initiatives "Laws governing local ballot measures in California") raised questions about how to interpret the constitutional voting requirements for special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives. 

California voters approved [Proposition 218](/California_Proposition_218,_Voter_Approval_Requirement_for_Local_Tax_Increases_Initiative_\(1996\) "California Proposition 218, Voter Approval Requirement for Local Tax Increases Initiative (1996)") in 1996, adding Article XIII C Voter Approval For Local Tax Levies to the California Constitution. The article includes the requirement that local governments may only enact, extend, or increase a special tax with a [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") of the electorate.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Following the passage of Proposition 218, the two-thirds supermajority vote requirement was applied to legislative referrals, referendums, and citizen initiatives. 

In August 2017, however, the [California Supreme Court](/California_Supreme_Court "California Supreme Court") ruled in *California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland* that one requirement contained in Article XIII C—that general taxes must be put on the ballot during general elections—did not apply to citizen initiatives. The court categorized taxes imposed by citizen initiatives as separate from taxes imposed by local governments. This ruling brought the [two-thirds (66.67%) vote](/Supermajority_requirement "Supermajority requirement") requirement into question for special taxes proposed through citizen initiatives. 

City and county officials in San Francisco argued that the court's 2017 decision meant that a simple majority—not a two-thirds supermajority—was required for the approval of local citizen initiatives, including tax measures that designate funds for specific purposes. Based on those arguments, the city certified the measures as approved. The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association filed a lawsuit against the city and county in August 2018, stating that the [Proposition C](/San_Francisco,_California,_Proposition_C,_Commercial_Rent_Tax_for_Childcare_and_Early_Education_\(June_2018\) "San Francisco, California, Proposition C, Commercial Rent Tax for Childcare and Early Education (June 2018)"), a commercial rent tax for childcare initiative, did not receive sufficient votes because it needed a two-thirds supermajority vote.[\[18\]](#cite_note-SFC-18) 

On January 27, 2021, the First District Court of Appeal ruled that the supermajority requirement did not apply to Proposition C and only applied to measures placed on the ballot by the city council, board of supervisors, or school board.[\[19\]](#cite_note-ruling-19) 

### California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)

*See also: [California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)](/California_Two-Thirds_Legislative_Vote_and_Voter_Approval_for_New_or_Increased_Taxes_Initiative_\(2024\) "California Two-Thirds Legislative Vote and Voter Approval for New or Increased Taxes Initiative (2024)")*

In 2024, the [Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association](/Howard_Jarvis_Taxpayers_Association "Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association") and California Business Roundtable qualified an initiative that would have amended the state constitution to define all state and local levies, charges, and fees as taxes and to require new state taxes proposed by the state legislature to be enacted via a two-thirds legislative vote and voter approval and new local taxes to be enacted via a two-thirds vote of the electorate.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) 

In June 2024, prior to the finalization of statewide ballots, the [California Supreme Court](/California_Supreme_Court "California Supreme Court") unanimously ruled that the 2024 initiative amounted to a revision of the state constitution and was therefore unconstitutional and could not go before voters in November.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21) 

### California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)

*See also: [California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)](/California_Two-Thirds_Vote_Requirement_for_Special_Taxes_and_Charter_City_Real_Estate_Transfer_Tax_Prohibition_Initiative_\(2026\) "California Two-Thirds Vote Requirement for Special Taxes and Charter City Real Estate Transfer Tax Prohibition Initiative (2026)")*

The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and California Business Roundtable qualified a ballot initiative for the 2026 election cycle that was withdrawn from the ballot following a legislative compromise, which included the passage of [ACA 22](#Path_to_the_ballot) placing Proposition 43 on the November 3 ballot. The initiative would have amended the state constitution to increase the vote requirement to pass citizen-initiated local special taxes from a simple majority (50%+1) to a two-thirds (66.67%) vote; prohibited charter cities from imposing their own real estate transfer taxes, whether for general or specific purposes, above the existing statutory rate of $0.275 per $500 of value; and invalidated any property-related special taxes previously adopted with an approval rate below two-thirds or real estate transfer taxes in charter cities. ACA 22 is not retroactive like the withdrawn ballot initiative.[\[22\]](#cite_note-text-22) 

On June 25, 2026, the [California State Legislature](/California_State_Legislature "California State Legislature") passed ACA 22 and withdrew a [separate ballot measure](/California_Vote_Requirements_for_Initiatives_Requiring_Supermajority_Votes_Amendment_\(2026\) "California Vote Requirements for Initiatives Requiring Supermajority Votes Amendment (2026)") that had previously been referred to the 2026 ballot. It would have required initiatives proposing supermajority vote thresholds to pass by the same vote threshold being proposed.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## How to cast a vote

*See also: [Voting in California](/Voting_in_California "Voting in California")*

*See below to learn more about current voter registration rules, identification requirements, and poll times in California.* 

How to vote in California

### Poll times

All polls in California are open from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Pacific Time. Anyone in line when the polls close must be allowed to vote.[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) 

### Registration

*Check your voter registration status **[here](https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/).***

To vote in California, an individual must be a U.S. citizen and California resident, not currently serving a state or federal prison term for the conviction of a felony, and not currently found mentally incompetent to vote by a court. A voter must be at least 18 years of age on election day. [Pre-registration](/Youth_pre-registration_laws_by_state "Youth pre-registration laws by state") is available for 16 and 17-year-olds. Pre-registered voters are automatically registered to vote when they turn 18.[\[27\]](#cite_note-careg-27) 

### Automatic registration

*See also: [Automatic voter registration](/Automatic_voter_registration "Automatic voter registration")*

California [automatically](/Automatic_voter_registration "Automatic voter registration") registers eligible individuals to vote when they complete a driver's license, identification (ID) card, or change of address transaction through the Department of Motor Vehicles.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) 

### Online registration

*See also: [Online voter registration](/Online_voter_registration "Online voter registration")*

California has implemented an online voter registration system. Residents can register to vote by visiting [this website](https://registertovote.ca.gov/). 

### Same-day registration

*See also: [Same-day voter registration](/Same-day_voter_registration "Same-day voter registration")*

California allows [same-day voter registration](/Same-day_voter_registration "Same-day voter registration"). 

Californians must be registered to vote at least 15 days before election day. If the registration deadline has passed for an upcoming election, voters may visit a county elections office, polling place, or vote center during the 14 days prior to, and including election day to conditionally register to vote and vote a provisional ballot, which are counted once county election officials have completed the voter registration verification process. The state refers to this process as same day voter registration.[\[29\]](#cite_note-casdreg-29)[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) 

### Residency requirements

To register to vote in California, you must be a resident of the state. State law does not specify a length of time for which you must have been a resident to be eligible. 

### Verification of citizenship

*See also: [Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States](/Laws_permitting_noncitizens_to_vote_in_the_United_States "Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States")*

California's constitution requires that voters be U.S. citizens. When registering to vote, proof of citizenship is not required. Individuals who become U.S. citizens less than 15 days before an election must bring proof of citizenship to their county elections office to register to vote in that election. An individual applying to register to vote must attest that they are a U.S. citizen under penalty of perjury.[\[29\]](#cite_note-casdreg-29) 

As of October 2026, two jurisdictions in California had [authorized noncitizen residents to vote](/Laws_permitting_noncitizens_to_vote_in_the_United_States "Laws permitting noncitizens to vote in the United States") for local board of education positions through local ballot measures. Only one of those jurisdictions, San Francisco, had implemented that law. Noncitizens voting for board of education positions must register to vote using a separate application from the state voter registration application.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) 

All 49 states with voter registration systems require applicants to declare that they are U.S. citizens in order to register to vote in state and federal elections, under penalty of perjury or other punishment.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Eight states — Alabama, Arizona, Kansas, Louisiana, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Utah, and Wyoming — have laws requiring individuals provide proof of citizenship at the time of voter registration, whether in effect or not. Three states, Florida, Georgia and Mississippi, require a person provide proof of citizenship if their citizenship status cannot be verified by other means.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33) One state, Ohio, requires proof of citizenship only when registering to vote at a Bureau of Motor Vehicles facility. In three states — California, Maryland, and Vermont — at least one local jurisdiction allows noncitizens to vote in some local elections. Noncitizens registering to vote in those elections must complete a voter registration application provided by the local jurisdiction and are not eligible to register as state or federal voters. 

### Verifying your registration

The secretary of state's [My Voter Status](https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/) website allows residents to check their voter registration status online. 

### Voter ID requirements

California does not require voters to present identification before casting a ballot in most cases. 

On September 29, 2024, Gov. [Gavin Newsom](/Gavin_Newsom "Gavin Newsom") (D) signed [SB 1174](https://legislation.ballotpedia.org/elections/bill/10007) into law prohibiting any jurisdiction in the state from adopting a local law that requires voters to present ID before voting.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34) 

The federal [Help America Vote Act](/Help_America_Vote_Act "Help America Vote Act") requires that individuals in all 50 states who register to vote by mail and who have not voted previously in a federal election in their state must provide either their driver's license or a paycheck, bank statement, current utility bill, or government document showing their name and address. Individuals voting by mail must include a copy of one of those documents with their absentee/mail-in ballot.[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) 

These requirements do not apply if an individual submitted a copy of their identification, their driver's license number or the last four digits of their Social Security number when registering to vote.
